summary: A Hebrew adjective comes AFTER its noun and agrees with it in three things: gender, number and definiteness. Every adjective has four forms — masculine and feminine, singular and plural: גָּדוֹל, גְּדוֹלָה, גְּדוֹלִים, גְּדוֹלוֹת “big”. The endings are those of the nouns (-ָה or -ֶת or -ִית for the feminine, -ִים and -וֹת for the plural), and what counts is the noun’s grammatical gender, not its ending: שֻׁלְחָנוֹת גְּדוֹלִים “big tables” (a masculine noun with -וֹת), עִיר יָפָה “a beautiful city” (a feminine noun without -ָה). The article decides between a phrase and a sentence. Attributive — “the big house” — repeats the article on the adjective: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל. Predicative — “the house is big” — leaves the adjective bare, and, as in every Hebrew present-tense sentence, there is no verb “is”: הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל. So one ה turns a sentence into a phrase. In the past and the future the verb הָיָה appears (הַבַּיִת הָיָה גָּדוֹל). Often the first vowel shortens in the longer forms (גָּדוֹל → גְּדוֹלָה, יָקָר → יְקָרָה); short adjectives double their last letter (קַל → קַלָּה, קָטָן → קְטַנָּה). Feelings of heat and cold, and easy and hard, are said impersonally with לְ: חַם לִי “I’m hot”, קַר לָהּ “she is cold”, קָשֶׁה לִי “it is hard for me” — the adjective stays masculine singular. There are no cases, so nothing else changes.

blocks.caption: Four forms; the endings are the noun endings -ָה / -ֶת / -ִית, -ִים, -וֹת. Adjectives in -ֶה turn it into -ָה; ־ִי takes ־ִית.

items.title: Attributive: “the big house” (a phrase)
points: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל — the big house: the article on both words
בַּבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל — in the big house: the adjective keeps its הַ

items.title: Predicative: “the house is big” (a sentence)
points: הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל — the house is big: no article on the adjective, no “is”
הַבַּיִת לֹא גָּדוֹל — the house is not big
הַבַּיִת הָיָה גָּדוֹל — the house was big

blocks.title: One ה makes the difference
blocks.text: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל = “the big house” (a phrase, waiting for a verb). הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל = “the house is big” (a complete sentence). Read the article on the adjective before you translate.

head: the article before the adjective
example
rows: הֶ before an unstressed חָ or עָ
blocks.caption: The same rules as for nouns (lesson 4).

head: pattern
masculine → feminine
examples
rows: יָקָר → יְקָרָה, צָעִיר → צְעִירָה, עָצוּב → עֲצוּבָה, זָקֵן → זְקֵנָה
קַל → קַלָּה, חַם → חַמָּה, קָטָן → קְטַנָּה
blocks.caption: You do not have to predict the forms: learn each adjective with its feminine — the drills ask for exactly that.

head: impersonal (with לְ)
meaning
rows: it is hard for me to get up
blocks.caption: The adjective stays masculine singular; the person is in לְ: never *אֲנִי חַם for “I’m hot”.

blocks.title: The noun’s gender, not its ending
blocks.text: שֻׁלְחָנוֹת גְּדוֹלִים (m., although -וֹת), נָשִׁים יָפוֹת (f., although -ִים), עִיר יָפָה (f., no ending), עֵינַיִם כְּחֻלּוֹת (f.). Check the gender of the noun in its word card.

blocks.title: Several adjectives
blocks.text: They follow one another, each agreeing: בַּיִת גָּדוֹל וְיָפֶה “a big and beautiful house”, הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל וְהַיָּפֶה. “Very” (מְאוֹד) comes after the adjective: יָפֶה מְאוֹד.

blocks.title: With a possessive
blocks.text: שֶׁלִּי can stand after the adjective or between: הַבַּיִת הֶחָדָשׁ שֶׁלִּי = הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי הֶחָדָשׁ “my new house” — the adjective keeps its article.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before you write an adjective
questions: Is it a phrase (“the big …”) or a sentence (“… is big”)?
What is the gender of the noun — and is it singular or plural?
Is the noun definite (הַ, a name, שֶׁל…)? Then the adjective takes הַ too.

askYourself: Where does the adjective go? → after the noun: בַּיִת גָּדוֹל.
Masculine or feminine noun (its gender, not its ending)? → גָּדוֹל or גְּדוֹלָה.
Is the noun definite? → in a phrase the adjective takes the article too: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל.
Is it a statement “X is Y”? → no article on the adjective and no verb in the present: הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל.
A feeling (hot, cold, easy, hard) of a person? → adjective + לְ: חַם לִי.
steps: Find the noun and its gender and number.
Choose the form of the adjective.
Decide phrase or sentence: article on the adjective only in the phrase.

traps: *הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל for “the big house” — that is “the house is big”; the phrase is הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל.
*בַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל — the article goes on both words or on none.
יָשָׁן is “old” for things; for people זָקֵן or, politely, מְבֻגָּר.
יָפֶה (m.) and יָפָה (f.) are written the same way; so are קָשֶׁה / קָשָׁה and כֵּהֶה / כֵּהָה.

quiz.why: In a phrase the adjective repeats the article. הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל is a sentence: “the house is big”.
No article on the adjective = a sentence; Hebrew has no “is” in the present.
The adjective follows the noun and takes its gender — עִיר is feminine although it has no -ָה.
שֻׁלְחָן is masculine; the -וֹת of its plural does not make it feminine.
Feeling hot or cold is impersonal: the adjective + לְ.
Before an unstressed חָ the article is הֶ: הֶחָדָשׁ (but הַחֲדָשָׁה).
יָשָׁן is for things; for people זָקֵן, or politely מְבֻגָּר.
Adjectives in ־ִי take ־ִית in the feminine.

seeAlso.note: Arabic is Hebrew’s twin here: the adjective follows the noun and copies its gender, number and definiteness (الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ “the big house”, الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ “the house is big”) — and also its case; non-human plurals take a feminine singular adjective.

German puts the adjective before the noun and gives it an ending only there (das große Haus, ein großes Haus); after sein it never changes (das Haus ist groß) — Hebrew changes it in both places, but only for gender and number.
Chinese adjectives are verbs: 房子很大 “the house is big” needs no 是, like Hebrew needs no “is”; before a noun they take 的 (很大的房子) and never change.
